intro: Throughout, log is the natural logarithm, E[⋅] and Var(⋅) are expectation and variance, and N(μ,σ2) denotes the density of a Gaussian with that mean and variance.
solutionIntro: Confirm the convention for log (natural, used throughout) and, where a question asks for a derivation, whether a standard identity may be quoted or should be shown from first principles; every derivation below is given in full regardless.

questions.q: Urn A holds 3 red balls and 1 blue ball; urn B holds 1 red ball and 3 blue balls. An urn is chosen by a fair coin toss, and one ball is drawn from it: the ball is red. Compute P(A∣red). A second ball is then drawn from the same urn without replacement (the first ball is not returned); compute the probability that this second ball is red too.
questions.a:
P(A∣red)=3/4, and the second ball is red with probability 1/2. By Bayes' theorem, P(red∣A)=3/4 and P(red∣B)=1/4, so P(red)=21​⋅43​+21​⋅41​=21​ and

P(A∣red)=P(red)P(red∣A)P(A)​=21​43​⋅21​​=43​.

For the second draw, condition on the urn: with probability 3/4 the urn is A, now holding 2 red and 1 blue after the first (red) ball is removed, so the second ball is red with probability 2/3; with probability 1/4 the urn is B, which after losing its only red ball holds 0 red and 3 blue, so the second ball is red with probability 0. Hence

P(2nd red∣1st red)=43​⋅32​+41​⋅0=21​.

questions.q: A fair coin is flipped repeatedly until the pattern HH first appears (two heads in a row); compute the expected number of flips. Do the same for the pattern HT, and explain why the two expectations differ.
questions.a: E[flips to HH]=6 and E[flips to HT]=4. Track one bit of state: 0 if the last flip was not H (or none has been seen yet), H if the last flip was H. For HH, from state 0 a flip is H with probability 1/2 (move to H) or T with probability 1/2 (stay at 0), so E0​=1+21​EH​+21​E0​; from state H, a flip is H with probability 1/2 (done) or T with probability 1/2 (back to 0 — the earlier H is wasted), so EH​=1+21​E0​. Solving gives EH​=4, E0​=6. For HT, the equation from state 0 is the same, E0​=1+21​EH​+21​E0​; but from state H, a flip is T with probability 1/2 (done) or H with probability 1/2 (stay at H — this new H can still start a match), so EH​=1+21​EH​, giving EH​=2, E0​=4. The two differ because HH overlaps itself (its one-letter prefix H is also its suffix): failing a near-miss (T after H) discards the H entirely and the search restarts from scratch, whereas failing a near-miss of HT (another H after H) discards nothing, since that new H is exactly as good a start as the first one was. Overlapping patterns are, on average, slower to wait for.

questions.q: Let X1​,…,Xn​ be independent Uniform(0,1) random variables. Compute E[maxi​Xi​] and E[mini​Xi​] as functions of n.
questions.a:
E[max]=n/(n+1) and E[min]=1/(n+1). The maximum has P(max≤x)=xn for x∈[0,1] (every Xi​≤x), hence density nxn−1 and

E[max]=∫01​x⋅nxn−1dx=n+1n​.

For the minimum, note that if U∼Uniform(0,1) then so is 1−U, so 1−mini​Xi​=maxi​(1−Xi​) has the same distribution as maxi​Xi​; taking expectations, 1−E[min]=n/(n+1), so E[min]=1/(n+1).

questions.q: A diagnostic test has sensitivity 99% (the probability of testing positive given the disease) and specificity 95% (the probability of testing negative given no disease). Disease prevalence in the tested population is 1%. Compute P(disease∣positive), and explain in one sentence why it is so much lower than the sensitivity.
questions.a:
P(disease∣positive)=1/6≈16.7%. By the law of total probability, P(positive)=P(pos∣D)P(D)+P(pos∣¬D)P(¬D)=0.99×0.01+0.05×0.99=0.0594, and Bayes' theorem gives

P(D∣positive)=0.05940.99×0.01​=0.05940.0099​=61​.

This is the base-rate effect: because the disease is rare, the healthy population (99% of everyone) is far larger than the diseased population, so even a small false-positive rate (5%) on that huge group produces more false positives (4.95% of the population) than there are true positives (0.99% of the population) — most positives are false alarms.

questions.q: Let X1​,…,Xn​ be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) samples from N(μ,σ2) with both parameters unknown. Derive the maximum-likelihood estimates μ^​ and σ^2, and show that σ^2 is a biased estimator of σ2, with E[σ^2]=nn−1​σ2.
questions.a:
μ^​=Xˉ=n1​∑i​Xi​ and σ^2=n1​∑i​(Xi​−Xˉ)2, and the latter is biased low by the factor (n−1)/n. The log-likelihood is ℓ(μ,σ2)=−2n​log(2πσ2)−2σ21​∑i​(Xi​−μ)2; setting ∂ℓ/∂μ=0 gives ∑i​(Xi​−μ)=0, i.e. μ^​=Xˉ, and setting ∂ℓ/∂σ2=0 at μ=μ^​ gives σ^2=n1​∑i​(Xi​−Xˉ)2. For the bias, expand around the true mean:

i∑​(Xi​−Xˉ)2=i∑​[(Xi​−μ)−(Xˉ−μ)]2=i∑​(Xi​−μ)2−n(Xˉ−μ)2,

using ∑i​(Xi​−μ)=n(Xˉ−μ). Taking expectations, E∑i​(Xi​−μ)2=nσ2 and E[n(Xˉ−μ)2]=nVar(Xˉ)=σ2, so E∑i​(Xi​−Xˉ)2=(n−1)σ2 and E[σ^2]=nn−1​σ2. The estimator spends one degree of freedom estimating μ with Xˉ, which is on average slightly closer to the sample than the true μ is, understating the spread; dividing by n−1 instead of n removes the bias exactly.

questions.q: Let y=Xw+ε with ε∼N(0,σ2I), and put an independent N(0,τ2) prior on each weight wj​. Show that the maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimate of w is the ridge-regression solution w^=argminw​∥Xw−y∥2+λ∥w∥2, for some λ that you should express in terms of σ2 and τ2. Then show that replacing the Gaussian prior with an independent Laplace prior on each wj​ makes the MAP estimate the L1-regularised (lasso) solution, and express its λ the same way.
questions.a:
λ=σ2/τ2 for ridge; for the Laplace prior with scale b, the L1 penalty has λ=2σ2/b. By Bayes' theorem the posterior satisfies p(w∣X,y)∝p(y∣X,w)p(w), so the MAP estimate maximises logp(y∣X,w)+logp(w), equivalently minimises its negative. The Gaussian likelihood gives −logp(y∣X,w)=2σ21​∥Xw−y∥2+const, and the Gaussian prior gives −logp(w)=2τ21​∥w∥2+const, so the MAP objective is

2σ21​∥Xw−y∥2+2τ21​∥w∥2,

and multiplying by 2σ2 (which does not change the minimiser) gives ∥Xw−y∥2+λ∥w∥2 with λ=σ2/τ2: exactly ridge regression. Replacing the prior with an independent Laplace(0,b) on each wj​, with density 2b1​e−∣wj​∣/b, gives −logp(w)=b1​∥w∥1​+const, so the MAP objective becomes 2σ21​∥Xw−y∥2+b1​∥w∥1​; multiplying by 2σ2 gives ∥Xw−y∥2+λ∥w∥1​ with λ=2σ2/b — the lasso. A Gaussian prior penalises large weights quadratically and shrinks every coordinate smoothly toward 0; a Laplace prior has a sharp peak at 0 (its penalty is not differentiable there), and the subgradient at that kink can hold a coordinate exactly at 0, which is why the lasso produces sparse solutions and ridge, generically, does not.

questions.q: Define the Kullback–Leibler divergence KL(p∥q) between two densities on the same space, and prove that KL(p∥q)≥0, with equality iff p=q almost everywhere. Give a two-point (Bernoulli) example with KL(p∥q)=KL(q∥p). Then consider fitting a single Gaussian q to a distribution p that is a two-component Gaussian mixture with well-separated modes: with a derivation, say what q minimising the forward divergence KL(p∥q) looks like ("mode-covering"), and, qualitatively, what q minimising the reverse divergence KL(q∥p) looks like ("mode-seeking").
questions.a:
KL(p∥q)=Ep​[logq(X)p(X)​]=∫p(x)logq(x)p(x)​dx≥0. For non-negativity, apply Jensen's inequality to the convex function −log with Y=q(X)/p(X) under X∼p: Ep​[Y]=∫p(x)p(x)q(x)​dx=∫q(x)dx=1 (over the support of p), so

KL(p∥q)=Ep​[−logY]≥−logEp​[Y]=−log1=0,

with equality iff Y is almost surely constant (since −log is strictly convex), i.e. q=p almost everywhere. Asymmetry: for p=Bernoulli(0.9), q=Bernoulli(0.5),

KL(p∥q)=0.9log0.50.9​+0.1log0.50.1​≈0.368,KL(q∥p)=0.5log0.90.5​+0.5log0.10.5​≈0.511,

which are not equal. For the Gaussian fit, write q=N(μ,σ2); minimising KL(p∥q)=−H(p)+H(p,q) over q is the same as minimising the cross-entropy H(p,q)=Ep​[−logq(X)]=21​log(2πσ2)+2σ2Ep​[(X−μ)2]​. This is minimised over μ at μ=Ep​[X] regardless of σ2, and then over σ2 at σ2=Varp​(X): forward KL is minimised by moment matching. As a concrete example, take p=21​N(−3,1)+21​N(3,1) (modes at ±3, each component with unit variance): then Ep​[X]=0 and Varp​(X)=Ep​[X2]=10 (each component has Var+mean2=1+9=10), so the forward-KL fit is N(0,10): wide and centred between the modes, in order to keep q positive wherever p is (else plog(p/q)→∞). The reverse divergence KL(q∥p)=Eq​[logq(X)−logp(X)] instead penalises q for putting mass where p is small, so it has no incentive to cover both modes; started near one mode, gradient-based fitting finds a q tightly wrapped around that single mode, close to its own mean and variance, rather than one covering both.

questions.q: You want to estimate a classifier's accuracy to within ±1 percentage point at 95% confidence, using the normal approximation to a Bernoulli proportion. How many i.i.d. test examples are needed in the worst case over the unknown true accuracy p? State the assumption needed for the normal approximation to be valid.
questions.a:
n≈9,604 in the worst case. For n i.i.d. Bernoulli(p) trials, the sample proportion p^​ has Var(p^​)=p(1−p)/n and, by the central limit theorem, is approximately N(p,p(1−p)/n) once n is large enough. A two-sided 95% interval has half-width z0.975​p(1−p)/n​ with z0.975​=1.96; setting this equal to the target margin E=0.01 and solving for n gives

n=E2z0.9752​p(1−p)​.

Since p(1−p)≤41​ for every p∈[0,1], with equality at p=1/2, the worst case is n=1.962×0.25/0.012=9,604. This requires n to be large enough that the normal approximation to the Binomial is accurate — in particular, that the examples are drawn i.i.d. with a fixed true accuracy p (no distribution shift across the test set) and that np and n(1−p) are both comfortably above about 5–10, which 9,604 satisfies for any p not extremely close to 0 or 1.

questions.q: Contrast the eigendecomposition and the singular value decomposition (SVD) of a real matrix X∈Rm×n: when does each exist? How do the singular values of X relate to the eigenvalues of X⊤X? How does the rank of X show up in its SVD? And, given a data matrix with rows as observations, how is principal component analysis (PCA) computed from the SVD of the centred data?
questions.a: The SVD X=UΣV⊤ (with U∈Rm×m, V∈Rn×n orthogonal, and Σ rectangular-diagonal with entries σ1​≥σ2​≥⋯≥0) exists for every real matrix of every shape, with no assumptions on X. An eigendecomposition A=QΛQ−1 requires a square matrix, is guaranteed to have real Λ and orthogonal Q only when A is symmetric (the spectral theorem), and can fail to exist at all for a general square matrix: the 2×2 matrix with a single 1 in the top-right corner and zeros elsewhere has the repeated eigenvalue 0 (algebraic multiplicity 2) but only a one-dimensional space of eigenvectors, so no invertible Q diagonalises it — a defective matrix. Since X⊤X=VΣ⊤U⊤UΣV⊤=V(Σ⊤Σ)V⊤ and Σ⊤Σ=diag(σi2​), this is exactly an eigendecomposition of the symmetric PSD matrix X⊤X: its eigenvalues are σi2​ and its eigenvectors are the columns of V, so σi​=λi​(X⊤X)​. Because U,V are invertible, rank(X)=rank(Σ), i.e. the number of nonzero singular values. For PCA, centre the data Xc​=X−Xˉ (subtract from each column its mean over the m rows) and take its SVD Xc​=UΣV⊤; then Xc⊤​Xc​=VΣ2V⊤ is (m−1) times the sample covariance matrix, so the principal directions are the columns of V, the explained variance along direction i is σi2​/(m−1), and the principal-component scores (the data projected onto those directions) are Xc​V=UΣ.

questions.q: Define positive semidefinite (PSD) for a real symmetric matrix. Prove that every covariance matrix is PSD. State and justify the relationship between a PSD Hessian and the convexity of a twice-differentiable function.
questions.a:
A symmetric matrix A∈Rn×n is PSD if x⊤Ax≥0 for every x∈Rn (equivalently, every eigenvalue is ≥0). For a random vector X with mean μ and covariance Σ=E[(X−μ)(X−μ)⊤], and any a∈Rn,

a⊤Σa=E[a⊤(X−μ)(X−μ)⊤a]=E[(a⊤(X−μ))2]≥0,

since this is the expectation of a squared scalar random variable; the same argument applies verbatim to the sample covariance, with E replaced by an average over the sample. So Σ is always PSD. A twice-differentiable f is convex on a convex domain if and only if ∇2f(x) is PSD at every point x in it. One direction: if f is convex, then for any direction v the function g(t)=f(x+tv) is convex (a convex function composed with an affine map), so g′′(0)=v⊤∇2f(x)v≥0 for every v, i.e. ∇2f(x) is PSD. Conversely, if ∇2f is PSD everywhere, Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder gives, for any x,y, f(y)=f(x)+∇f(x)⊤(y−x)+21​(y−x)⊤∇2f(ξ)(y−x) for some ξ on the segment between them; the last term is ≥0 by assumption, so f(y)≥f(x)+∇f(x)⊤(y−x) for all x,y, which is exactly the first-order characterisation of convexity.

questions.q: Derive ∇x​(x⊤Ax) for x∈Rn, A∈Rn×n; ∇W​∥XW−Y∥F2​, the gradient of the squared Frobenius norm (the sum of squared entries) of XW−Y, for X∈Rm×p, W∈Rp×k, Y∈Rm×k; and the Jacobian of the softmax function s=softmax(z) with respect to z∈RK.
questions.a: ∇x​(x⊤Ax)=(A+A⊤)x; ∇W​∥XW−Y∥F2​=2X⊤(XW−Y); the softmax Jacobian is diag(s)−ss⊤. Writing x⊤Ax=∑i,j​Aij​xi​xj​ and differentiating with respect to xk​: ∂k​(x⊤Ax)=∑j​Akj​xj​+∑i​Aik​xi​=(Ax)k​+(A⊤x)k​, so ∇x​(x⊤Ax)=(A+A⊤)x (equal to 2Ax when A is symmetric). For the second, write R=XW−Y and use differentials: d∥R∥F2​=dtr(R⊤R)=2tr(R⊤dR)=2tr(R⊤XdW)=2tr((X⊤R)⊤dW), and since d∥R∥F2​=tr(G⊤dW) defines the gradient G, reading off gives G=2X⊤R=2X⊤(XW−Y). For the softmax, si​=ezi​/Z with Z=∑k​ezk​; by the quotient rule, ∂si​/∂zj​=δij​ezi​/Z−ezi​ezj​/Z2=δij​si​−si​sj​=si​(δij​−sj​), which in matrix form is J=diag(s)−ss⊤ — symmetric, and with rows summing to 0 (perturbing every logit by the same amount leaves softmax unchanged).

questions.q: For f(x)=21​x⊤Ax with A∈Rn×n symmetric positive definite, with eigenvalues 0<λ1​≤⋯≤λn​=λmax​, consider gradient descent xt+1​=xt​−η∇f(xt​) with step size η=1/λmax​. Show that the error contracts geometrically along each eigenvector of A, with the i-th eigen-direction shrinking by a factor 1−λi​/λmax​ per step, so that the slowest-converging direction shrinks by 1−1/κ, where κ=λmax​/λmin​ is the condition number. Explain why a large condition number slows convergence, and how feature normalisation or preconditioning helps.
questions.a:
The minimiser is x⋆=0, so the error is xt​ itself. ∇f(x)=Ax, so xt+1​=(I−ηA)xt​ with η=1/λmax​. Diagonalise A=QΛQ⊤ and write yt​=Q⊤xt​ for the coordinates of xt​ in the eigenbasis; then yt+1​=(I−ηΛ)yt​ is diagonal, so coordinate by coordinate,

yt+1,i​=(1−λmax​λi​​)yt,i​⟹yt,i​=(1−λmax​λi​​)ty0,i​.

Every coordinate contracts geometrically, at a rate that depends only on its own eigenvalue: the direction of λmax​ has 1−λmax​/λmax​=0 and reaches exactly 0 after a single step, while the direction of λmin​ has the largest (slowest) contraction factor 1−λmin​/λmax​=1−1/κ. Because the error norm ∥xt​∥ is a sum of these per-direction terms, once the faster directions have died away it is dominated by the λmin​ term, so ∥xt​∥/∥xt−1​∥→1−1/κ: the overall rate is set by the worst-conditioned direction, however fast the others converge. When κ≫1 (ill-conditioning — some directions of f are much flatter than others), 1−1/κ is close to 1 and convergence along the flat directions is extremely slow, even though the step size is tuned optimally for the steepest direction; a smaller step would only slow the flat directions further, and a larger one helps very little: any step above 2/λmax​ diverges along the steepest direction, and even the best fixed step η=2/(λmin​+λmax​) only improves the slowest factor to (κ−1)/(κ+1), still close to 1. Feature normalisation (rescaling inputs to comparable variance) and preconditioning (replacing A with P−1A for some P≈A, e.g. a diagonal or block approximation of the Hessian) both act by shrinking the ratio between the largest and smallest curvature, pushing κ toward 1 so that every direction contracts at a similar, fast rate.

def lasso_ista(X, y, lam, n_iter=4000):
    lipschitz = 2 * np.linalg.eigvalsh(X.T @ X).max()
    step = 1.0 / lipschitz
    w = np.zeros(X.shape[1])
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        w = w - step * 2 * X.T @ (X @ w - y)
        w = np.sign(w) * np.maximum(np.abs(w) - step * lam, 0.0)   # proximal step: soft-thresholding
    return w

grid = np.linspace(-20.0, 20.0, 8001)
dx = grid[1] - grid[0]
p_grid = mixture_pdf(grid)


def forward_kl_obj(params):                                  # KL(p || q), q = N(mu, exp(log_sigma)^2)
    mu, log_sigma = params
    q = np.clip(stats.norm.pdf(grid, mu, math.exp(log_sigma)), 1e-300, None)
    return np.sum(p_grid * (np.log(np.clip(p_grid, 1e-300, None)) - np.log(q))) * dx


def reverse_kl_obj(params):                                   # KL(q || p)
    mu, log_sigma = params
    q = stats.norm.pdf(grid, mu, math.exp(log_sigma))
    qc, pc = np.clip(q, 1e-300, None), np.clip(p_grid, 1e-300, None)
    return np.sum(q * (np.log(qc) - np.log(pc))) * dx

# ---- Q12: gradient descent on a quadratic, contraction along each eigendirection of A
Q12o, _ = np.linalg.qr(rng.standard_normal((4, 4)))
lambdas = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 8.0, 25.0])                        # lambda_max = 25 -> kappa = 25
A12 = Q12o @ np.diag(lambdas) @ Q12o.T
eta12 = 1.0 / lambdas.max()
x = rng.standard_normal(4)
coords = [Q12o.T @ x]
for _ in range(200):
    x = x - eta12 * (A12 @ x)
    coords.append(Q12o.T @ x)
Y12 = np.array(coords)                                            # (T + 1, 4): coordinates in the eigenbasis
predicted = 1 - lambdas / lambdas.max()
for t in range(len(Y12) - 1):
    ratio = np.divide(Y12[t + 1], Y12[t], out=np.full(4, np.nan), where=np.abs(Y12[t]) > 1e-12)
    ok = ~np.isnan(ratio)
    assert np.allclose(ratio[ok], predicted[ok], atol=1e-8)
assert math.isclose(Y12[1, np.argmax(lambdas)], 0.0, abs_tol=1e-10)   # top eigen-direction: exactly 0 after 1 step
late_ratio = np.linalg.norm(Y12[-1]) / np.linalg.norm(Y12[-2])
assert math.isclose(late_ratio, 1 - lambdas.min() / lambdas.max(), rel_tol=1e-6)   # dominated by 1 - 1/kappa
# 1/lambda_max is not the stability limit: every step below 2/lambda_max still contracts all directions, and the
# best fixed step 2/(lambda_min + lambda_max) only improves the slowest factor to (kappa - 1)/(kappa + 1)
kappa12 = lambdas.max() / lambdas.min()
assert np.abs(1 - 1.9 / lambdas.max() * lambdas).max() < 1 < np.abs(1 - 2.1 / lambdas.max() * lambdas).max()
assert math.isclose(np.abs(1 - 2 / (lambdas.min() + lambdas.max()) * lambdas).max(), (kappa12 - 1) / (kappa12 + 1))
